title: Major lower-limb amputation: level, consent and rehabilitation

guidelineVersions: BACPAR Clinical guidelines for the pre and post operative physiotherapy management of adults with lower limb amputations, 3rd edition (2025)
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Acute limb ischaemia, the emergency counterpart to this chronic presentation
Peripheral arterial examination of the lower limb, used to assess viability before amputation
Diabetic foot examination: neuropathy, ischaemia and infection, a common route to this decision

brief.scenario: Mr Alan Prescott, 68, has severe chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and is being considered for major lower-limb amputation.
brief.task: Discuss how you would approach consent, how the amputation level is chosen, and what happens after surgery.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Confirm nothing revascularisable remains, then let tissue viability and function (not just anatomical length) pick the level, then plan rehabilitation from before the operation.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming the lowest possible level is always best, or treating consent as covering only bleeding and infection.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I would first establish the indication and confirm vascular and multidisciplinary options have been considered."

flow: Confirm the indication and options considered

grid.label: Confirming the indication
grid.fail: Moves straight to discussing amputation level without checking whether revascularisation or other options were considered.
grid.pass: Establishes the indication for amputation and confirms that vascular and multidisciplinary options have been explored first.
grid.high: Notes this should have been discussed at a vascular multidisciplinary meeting, given the irreversible nature of the decision.

grid.label: Consent discussion
grid.fail: Describes consent as covering only bleeding and infection.
grid.pass: Discusses the operation, alternatives, risks including pain and phantom limb pain, wound complications, the possibility of further surgery, mobility implications and rehabilitation.
grid.high: Frames these as a two-way discussion about what matters most to this patient's daily life and goals, not a list read out to them.

grid.label: Choosing the amputation level
grid.fail: States the level should simply be as low (distal) as possible.
grid.pass: States the level is selected according to tissue viability, perfusion, infection, likelihood of healing and the functional potential of the remaining limb.
grid.high: Explains a higher level that heals reliably and rehabilitates well can outperform a lower level that fails to heal or cannot be fitted properly.

grid.label: Preoperative rehabilitation planning
grid.fail: Says rehabilitation is something to think about only after the wound has healed.
grid.pass: Involves the specialist amputee rehabilitation team, including physiotherapy, before surgery where possible.
grid.high: Adds that pre-operative assessment considers mobility goals, the contralateral limb, and psychological preparation, which shapes the rehabilitation plan made afterwards.

grid.label: Postoperative care
grid.fail: Names only wound care as the postoperative priority.
grid.pass: Lists pain management including phantom limb pain, wound care, nutrition, VTE prevention, pressure area care, psychological support and rehabilitation.
grid.high: Explains phantom limb pain is addressed with a structured rehabilitation approach, and links psychological support explicitly to adjustment after limb loss.

grid.label: Function versus anatomical length (safety-critical)
grid.fail: States prosthesis fitting alone will resolve function regardless of level or wound healing.
grid.pass: States functional outcome depends as much on healing and rehabilitation potential as on how much limb length is preserved.
grid.high: Adds that disease in the contralateral limb is assessed too, since it affects overall mobility and the choice of prosthesis and rehabilitation plan.

failures.move: Proceeding straight to level and technique without confirming the indication and that alternatives were considered.
failures.consequence: An irreversible operation goes ahead without the multidisciplinary safeguard it needs.

failures.move: Limiting consent to bleeding and infection.
failures.consequence: He is not prepared for phantom limb pain, mobility change or the possibility of further surgery.

failures.move: Choosing the lowest possible level regardless of viability.
failures.consequence: A stump that fails to heal, requiring revision surgery and delaying rehabilitation.

failures.move: Leaving rehabilitation planning until after the wound has healed.
failures.consequence: Time preparing him physically and psychologically for recovery is lost.

failures.move: Assuming a prosthesis alone will restore function.
failures.consequence: Poor healing or unaddressed contralateral disease means the prosthesis cannot be used well.

recovery.when: You blank on what consent should cover
recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around the indication, the procedure, its risks and alternatives, and what recovery will involve.
Yes — I'd also consider the contralateral limb and involve rehabilitation early, since that shapes the whole recovery.

knowledge.fact: Amputation level is chosen on tissue viability, perfusion, infection, likelihood of healing and functional potential, not simply the lowest possible level.
Consent covers the operation, alternatives, risks (including phantom limb pain), wound complications, further surgery, mobility change and rehabilitation.
The specialist amputee rehabilitation team, including physiotherapy, prosthetics, occupational therapy and psychological support, is involved before surgery where possible and continues afterwards.

recall.think: An irreversible decision made without confirming options or planning rehabilitation.
recall.say: "The level is chosen on viability, healing and function, not maximum length."
do: Confirm indication and that alternatives were considered
Consent for phantom pain, mobility change and further surgery

numbers.meaning: Current BACPAR pre- and post-operative amputee rehabilitation guideline

recall.trap: Assuming the lowest possible level, or a prosthesis alone, guarantees the best function.
recall.finish: Level chosen for viability and function; rehabilitation and psychological support started early and continued postoperatively.

partner.opening: Mr Prescott, 68, has severe chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and is being considered for major lower-limb amputation. "How would you approach consent?"

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks whether revascularisation has been considered
reveals.finding: He has been discussed at the vascular MDT; no further revascularisation options remain.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the contralateral limb
reveals.finding: The other leg also has significant peripheral arterial disease, currently stable.

push.question: How do you choose the level?
push.expect: Tissue viability, perfusion, infection, healing likelihood and functional potential.

push.question: What happens after surgery?
push.expect: Pain including phantom limb pain, wound care, nutrition, VTE prevention, pressure areas, psychological support, rehabilitation.

push.question: Why not always preserve maximum limb length?
push.expect: The level must balance tissue viability, healing and the patient's expected functional outcome.

curveballs.prompt: He asks whether he'll definitely walk again with a prosthesis.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains this depends on healing, fitness, rehabilitation and the contralateral limb, and cannot be guaranteed, rather than promising a prosthesis will resolve everything.

curveballs.prompt: He says he's worried about pain after the operation but no one has mentioned phantom limb pain.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains phantom limb pain explicitly as part of consent and describes the rehabilitation approach used to manage it.

curveballs.prompt: The surgical team wants to proceed to theatre this week without rehabilitation input.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Requests specialist amputee rehabilitation involvement before surgery where feasible, rather than deferring it to after the wound heals.
